intro: A short falling figure generates much of Mendelssohn’s concert overture. How does it remain recognisable as harmony, register and orchestral weight change around it?
question: How much music can grow from one falling figure?

sections.label: Return
sections.mNote: falling figure recovers B minor within a decorated recapitulation

sections.label: Quiet major-key passage
sections.mNote: second subject now in B major, with exposed clarinet

relations.label: The lyrical phrase is restated
relations.basis: The lyrical second-subject group in the exposition reiterates its broad phrase over continuing accompanimental motion. Both measured spans lie in the D-major contrast identified near 120 s, not in the later recapitulation. CENS diagonal mean 0.927, sustained 19 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 27 s (cache/form/mendelssohn-hebrides.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Begin with the lower line
cues.text: The opening idea is a short falling figure, introduced in the lower orchestral register. Follow its shape and the space before it: those small features offer landmarks as the music expands beyond the opening passage.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the falling figure and its low-register setting; this note does not time an instrumental entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Before entering the cave
cues.text: On 7 August 1829 Mendelssohn wrote a family letter containing the overture’s opening twenty-one bars. He visited Fingal’s Cave the following day, so this musical sketch preceded the celebrated visit rather than being composed inside the cave.
cues.evidence: Yale’s Art and Music in Britain exhibition reproduces the dated letter and establishes the order of the two events.

cues.title: A figure beneath the melody
cues.text: Throughout the opening, follow the short descending figure rather than only the highest line. Its repeated shape offers continuity even as the harmonies and orchestral layers around it change.
cues.evidence: The score develops the opening figure across the exposition; no new entrance is claimed at this display time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A longer singing phrase
cues.text: The lyrical second subject offers a longer line than the opening figure. Compare the broad melody with the continuing movement underneath it: a slower melodic pace need not bring the accompaniment to rest.
cues.evidence: The score and Duncan Gillies’s programme note distinguish the longer second subject; its placement here is an estimate from the opening span’s proportions.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first large crest
cues.text: The latter part of the exposition gathers orchestral weight. Listen for how the compact material can support a sustained stronger passage, rather than assuming that a large peak requires a wholly new theme.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises across 3:00–3:20; the 3:20–3:35 windows include the recording’s strongest sustained passage.

cues.title: An overture without an opera
cues.text: The Hebrides was written for the concert hall, not to introduce a stage work. It was first performed in London on 14 May 1832, and Mendelssohn continued revising it after that performance.
cues.evidence: Duncan Gillies’s Portobello Orchestra programme note records the concert premiere and subsequent revision.

cues.title: Developing familiar fragments
cues.text: In the development, familiar fragments are moved and recombined rather than replaced by a new principal tune. Listen for the opening contour in less settled surroundings; recognition matters as much as novelty here.
cues.evidence: The score has a sonata-form development; several audio changes around 4:16–4:40 support an approximate location, not a formal boundary by themselves.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass changes the meaning
cues.text: Follow the low notes beneath the recurring material. A familiar contour can acquire a different harmonic meaning over a new bass, allowing the overture to move away from its starting point without abandoning its vocabulary.
cues.evidence: This is a listening guide to the development’s use of recurring material, not a machine-derived chord label.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Turner visits Staffa
cues.text: Turner visited Staffa in 1831, two years after Mendelssohn. His painting Staffa, Fingal’s Cave, dated around 1831–32, places a modern steamship beside the ancient geological formation.
cues.evidence: The Yale Center for British Art’s record B1978.43.14 documents the visit, dating and steamship.

cues.title: Colour and overall level
cues.text: This stretch contains a change from brighter to darker sound without a comparable disappearance in level. Listen separately to the upper-frequency edge of the sound and the strength of the musical line.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a substantial shift towards lower-frequency sound around 6:00–6:05, with a smaller change in relative level.

cues.title: Short attacks, longer build-up
cues.text: In this part of the development, repeated attacks accompany a gradual increase in level. Try following the small rhythmic units and the longer rise at the same time: they shape the passage at different scales.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks become more frequent around 6:25–6:45 while relative level rises towards 7:00.

cues.title: Recognising the opening ground
cues.text: The later return brings the opening material back into the overture’s home-key argument. Compare it with your memory of the first passage: a recapitulation restores familiar material without necessarily replaying everything unchanged.
cues.evidence: The score establishes the recapitulation; the withdrawal around 7:35 supports only an approximate location in this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quieter exposed stretch
cues.text: Through the quieter passage, follow how the line stays connected between attacks. With less overall weight, the shape of the phrase and the balance between parts become useful points of attention.
cues.evidence: The relative level falls across 8:15–8:30, reaching one of the recording’s lowest non-terminal stretches.

cues.title: Building a musical institution
cues.text: Mendelssohn took charge of Leipzig’s Gewandhaus concerts in 1835. In 1843 he founded the Leipzig Conservatoire; orchestral direction and musical education accompanied his work as a composer.
cues.evidence: The Munich Philharmonic’s biography records the 1835 appointment and 1843 conservatoire foundation.

cues.title: The closing drive
cues.text: The closing span moves from the quiet passage towards a stronger, more articulated texture. Listen for the familiar figures within the larger sound rather than treating the ending as a separate episode.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows renewed activity around 9:30 and a substantial relative-level rise by 9:50.

cues.title: Separate attacks within the whole
cues.text: Within the fuller closing music, listen for the space between short notes. Coordinated articulation can make a figure recognisable even when several orchestral parts contribute to the surrounding sound.
cues.evidence: This is an articulation-focused listening invitation; the analysis does not identify which instruments make individual attacks.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The last rise and withdrawal
cues.text: The final span gathers force before drawing back. Keep the opening figure in memory as the texture contracts: the overture does not sustain its greatest orchestral weight to the end.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises towards 10:55, then declines through 11:10–11:20.

cues.title: A reduced closing scale
cues.text: The closing passage brings the music back to a smaller scale after the full-orchestra surges. Compare that contraction with the compact, low-register idea that opened the overture.
cues.evidence: The score’s reduced close is supported by the recording’s lower relative level and darker sound in its final passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass figure makes room for song
transitions.how: The transition redirects the B minor opening towards D major, its relative major, and reduces the force of the preceding gestures. Cellos and bassoons carry the longer second subject while the strings maintain smaller undulating movement around it. The low register therefore remains important, but it changes function: the compact falling figure gives way to a sustained melodic span. The underlying pulse continues, so the broader tune sounds slower than its accompaniment without requiring a separate slow movement.
transitions.evidence: The lyrical-contrast marker is 2:00. Analysis shows a quieter region around 1:50–2:15 and D-major confirmation later in the paragraph. The score supplies the relative-major second subject, its low melodic scoring and moving accompaniment; the provisional relation matches phrases at 2:01–2:20 and 2:28–2:47. The initial entrance remains approximate.

transitions.title: The falling figure loses a fixed destination
transitions.how: The exposition’s full orchestral writing subsides, and the short opening material becomes exposed again. D major no longer serves as a settled destination: fragments of the falling figure are repeated against changing bass harmonies and passed between orchestral layers. Mendelssohn keeps the figure’s rhythm recognisable while shortening the listener’s horizon from a complete tune to its component gestures. The reduced texture makes those harmonic changes audible before another large build begins.
transitions.evidence: The development marker is 4:16, also a measured boundary, after the marked fall in relative level around 4:00–4:10. Further boundaries occur at 4:20, 4:34 and 4:40. The score’s developmental fragmentation and changing harmony supply the explanation; the audio’s passing key estimates are not turned into a chord sequence.

transitions.title: F♯ gives the opening figure its ground
transitions.how: The development’s accumulated motion is directed onto F♯, the dominant of B minor. As that pressure relaxes into the home key, the opening’s falling figure becomes recognisable as a beginning again, not another sequential fragment. The bass supplies the tonal return while the orchestral texture contracts from the preceding surge. Mendelssohn restores the original material without erasing the agitation accumulated around it; the recapitulation can be more decorated than its first statement.
transitions.evidence: The return marker is 7:35. Analysis shows F♯-based sound in the preceding 7:15–7:30 span, followed by a substantial level drop and B-centred sound at 7:35. The score supplies the dominant preparation and B-minor recapitulation. The relations file finds no long matching path for this return, so neither its precise onset nor literal identity is claimed.

transitions.title: A major third softens the home key
transitions.how: The returning second subject is redirected from the exposition’s D major to B major, the major form of the home tonic. D♯ replaces B minor’s D♮, while F♯ dominant harmony prepares the new colouring. The clarinet’s exposed singing line and the reduced accompaniment make this a different scale of return from the orchestral first subject. The longer melodic span remains identifiable even though its register, instrumental voice and tonal destination have changed.
transitions.evidence: The quiet-major marker is 8:30, within the report’s low-level span after the 8:22 boundary. F♯-major estimates there are compatible with dominant preparation, not proof of the melody’s key. The score supplies the B-major second-subject return and clarinet scoring; its individual entrance is not aligned.

transitions.title: The shorter figure takes back the pulse
transitions.how: The quiet B-major paragraph gives way to renewed short-note activity and the home key’s minor colouring. D♮ replaces D♯ as B minor reasserts itself. The broader tune yields to compact figures related to the opening, while more of the orchestra joins the drive and the bass again directs emphatic cadential motion. The join is a change in scale and articulation: the material that sustained a long song is replaced by gestures that can be repeated and accumulated.
transitions.evidence: The closing-drive boundary is 9:30, also a measured change with renewed attacks and brighter sound; level rises substantially by 9:50. The score supplies the return of short closing figures and B-minor direction. Pitch estimates corroborate the broad region but do not time the modal inflection.

transitions.title: The opening survives in smaller fragments
transitions.how: Mendelssohn removes the full orchestra’s weight instead of making the final B minor louder. The opening figure is reduced to brief wind recollections, with the clarinet particularly exposed, and the strings’ final plucked punctuation leaves space around the cadence. The bass confirms the tonic while the upper material loses its earlier continuity. A motif that generated the overture now supplies its last fragments; the closing contraction is written into the scoring, not merely a fading recording.
transitions.evidence: The withdrawal marker is 11:10. Relative level and brightness fall through 11:10–11:20 after the late crest. The score supplies the reduced wind recollections, plucked string ending and B-minor close; the measured decay does not identify exact releases or instrumental entries.

facts: Piano with Ludwig Berger; composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter in Berlin
Music director, Düsseldorf, 1833–35; Gewandhaus conductor, Leipzig, from 1835; founder of Leipzig Conservatoire, 1843
Brother of Fanny Hensel; married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children
Symphonies, concert overtures, concertos, oratorios, chamber music and Songs without Words
composer.background:
Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 and grew up in Berlin, where his father Abraham’s banking wealth supported an unusually extensive education. His grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; Felix and his siblings were baptised as Christians in 1816, and the family used the additional surname Bartholdy. He studied piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, alongside his elder sister Fanny. The family’s concerts extended their classroom education with repeated opportunities to hear their own music, revise it and discuss it with experienced performers.

Zelter’s teaching joined Bach’s counterpoint to classical forms. The boy wrote string symphonies, concertos and chamber works before the pieces usually treated as his starting point. At sixteen he composed the E♭ major Octet, Op. 20, for four violins, two violas and two cellos. Its eight independent parts create different densities inside one ensemble: the first violin’s long ascent, the other instruments’ pulsing accompaniments and the finale’s fugal entries continually reshape the texture. The scherzo’s soft, rapid articulation became a recurrent technical problem in his later orchestral writing.
composer.epithet: A composer-conductor who turned quicksilver string writing, Bachian counterpoint and remembered landscapes into tightly organised concert music.
